By “Islamic philosophy,” then, ʿAbd al-Rāziq means all intellectual work produced within “Islamic” thought that contains elements of philosophical reasoning, including rational methods of inference and the organization of detailed arguments under broader principles.
ʿAbd al-Rāziq defends the originality of the Muslim philosophers—figures such as al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and Ibn Rushd, whom al-Nashshār describes as imitators of earlier masters.
He also rejects the racial theories used by some Western scholars when discussing these philosophers, especially attempts to divide thought into a “Semitic mind” and an “Aryan mind.”

“By the twentieth century, the idea of bringing Semitism and Aryanism into judgments about Islamic philosophy had almost disappeared, as the theory of Semitism and Aryanism itself weakened and lost much of its scientific support.”
There are also two points where ʿAbd al-Rāziq moves beyond his own traditionalist method and comes close to a historical one.
The first is that he is willing to use the term “philosophers of Islam” even for philosophers who were not Muslims, and to call their philosophy “Islamic”:
“Those who practiced philosophy under Islam, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, are called the philosophers of Islam, and their philosophy is called Islamic philosophy in the conventional sense...”
The second is that he supports the name “Islamic philosophy” partly because the people who practiced this philosophy themselves used that name.
From this he reaches an important conclusion:

“For all these reasons, we believe that we should call the philosophy we are discussing by the name its own people gave it: ‘Islamic philosophy,’ meaning that it arose in the lands of Islam and under the rule of the Islamic state, regardless of the religion or language of those who produced it.”
On these two points, and especially in this final explanation, ʿAbd al-Rāziq moves beyond his original method toward another one that comes close, as we have said, to a historical approach.
But this shift remains limited because the heart of his argument is still not historical.
At its core, his analysis rests on two ideas.
First, he ties “Islamic philosophy” to Islamic doctrine and law.
Second, he has a particular view of the relationship between religion and the heritage of the “philosophers of Islam.”
For him, this relationship is based on reconciliation between religion and philosophy and on the idea that religion and philosophy share “one truth and one goal.”

This is the heart of the issue not only for ʿAbd al-Rāziq, but for other modern thinkers whose understanding of the heritage rests on a bourgeois ideological position that also shapes their views of contemporary questions more generally.

Their insistence that the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage as a whole had a religious and “reconciliatory” character, and their insistence that all its philosophers accepted a “unity of truth and unity of purpose” between religion and philosophy, does not mainly come from a failure to study the texts deeply enough or to recognize their historical setting.

Its deeper source is an intellectual outlook that can see the heritage only from its religious and metaphysical side because it follows—sometimes consciously, sometimes unconsciously—the dominant ideological structure of bourgeois thought.
One aim of this book is to challenge the “myth” that this heritage was essentially based on reconciliation between religion and philosophy.

It will also try to remove the surface appearance that has led people to imagine that the “philosophers of Islam,” or at least the major ones among them, accepted the idea that religion and philosophy share “one truth and one goal.”
Ibrāhīm Madkūr also tried to move beyond both the traditionalist method and the Western Orientalist method toward what he called a “historical method.”
He noticed the weaknesses in existing studies of the heritage of “Islamic philosophy” and the mistaken assumptions on which many of those studies were based.
He therefore concluded that researchers needed to rely on “the historical method” if they wanted to correct these weaknesses and challenge those assumptions.
This is a valuable proposal from a major scholar in the field of modern philosophical studies, and it deserves to be treated positively.
That remains true even if we set aside Madkūr’s unconvincing attempt to excuse the assumptions of Western researchers.

He argues that these assumptions arose “mostly because they were formed before a complete study had been made, and because they were not drawn directly from Islamic thought in its original sources, but were instead suggested by a distorted picture found in the Latin manuscripts then in circulation.”

He also writes that “some historians of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries discussed Muslim intellectual life without knowing the language, or without having enough Arabic sources available to them.”
In reality, Western scholars, including Orientalists, did not reach their conclusions simply because they were “ignorant” of the original sources or lacked knowledge of Arabic.
The original sources of the heritage have often been more available to them than to us.
And the many Western scholars who know Arabic are no less proficient in it than many contemporary Arab researchers themselves.
Dr. Madkūr must know this very well.
So, leaving aside this “explanation,” which does not change the historical reality, we can still view his call for a “historical method” positively.
But what exactly does Madkūr mean by this method?
He says that Islamic thought should be

“presented in itself and studied realistically in light of the foreign ideas that reached the Muslims and on the basis of the questions and discussions produced within the Islamic environment itself. It should be known directly through those who created it and expressed it, so that it can be understood as it truly was and properly grasped. Its stages of development should then be followed: its origin, growth, completion, and maturity, and the extent of its influence on later generations and schools should be shown.”
He also says that the researcher should try, as far as possible, to enter into the life of the people of the past.
Ideas should not be studied in isolation from one another.
The philosopher being studied should be placed properly within his environment.
The researcher should understand the philosopher’s formation and how it was connected to the ideas of his time.
His views should not be separated from other connected areas of Islamic culture.
Historical periods should not be divided by artificial boundaries.
And history should not be turned into a set of hypotheses with no connection to reality.
These are the main outlines of Madkūr’s “historical method,” scattered throughout the introduction to his book.
If we bring them together and treat them as a single whole, they provide a sound basis for historical research into the heritage.

At the same time, we can already see signs that Madkūr’s idea of “historical method” is mainly concerned with the internal history of ideas and thinkers themselves. It sometimes seems closer to historical editing of texts and to intellectual biography than to a history of the wider society in which those ideas arose.
For the moment, however, we will not base our judgment on these hints. It would be too early.
Looking only at the method as he presents it in theory, we have to view it positively and consider it a new attempt to produce a modern understanding of the heritage.
That is true at the formal and theoretical level.
But whether its intellectual and ideological starting point is sound can only be decided by looking at how the method is actually applied.
Madkūr gives the book we are discussing the slogan “A Method and Its Application.” In the introduction, he promises that applying the method will confirm and clarify it.

When he discusses the relationship between Islamic and Greek philosophy, he rejects theories claiming that Islamic philosophy was simply a copy of Aristotle, as Renan argued, or of Neoplatonism, as Duhem claimed.

In arguing against these views, he points out that Muslim philosophers lived in an environment and under conditions different from those of other philosophers, and that it is a mistake to ignore the effect of those conditions on their ideas and theories.
“The Islamic world was therefore able to form a philosophy of its own, one that developed in harmony with its religious and social foundations...”
All of this suggests that we are about to see a serious practical application to match the serious theoretical proposal.
But we run into the problem from the very first step.

Madkūr begins his practical application by discussing the “theory of happiness and union” and its relation to Islamic Sufism. He then examines Islamic Sufism itself and, after that, al-Fārābī’s Sufism.
Sufism may be one of the best possible tests of a historical method.

Its historical character can only be uncovered by someone who takes the scientific core of that method seriously, rather than stopping at a formal version of history concerned only with “the internal history of the thinker and his thought.”
Sufism is certainly subjective in one sense: it is an inner experience lived by the individual Sufi.
But in reality, it is also a social phenomenon because it expresses an indirect response to a particular social reality.
This is why Sufism takes different forms and develops different features under different kinds of social relations, political conditions, and systems of power.

Studying Sufism in any particular society is therefore a demanding test. The facts themselves reveal how strong or weak a research method is, and they also reveal its intellectual and ideological character.
This is exactly what we find when Madkūr applies his “historical” method to Sufism.
From the first step, as we have said, the method disappoints us.
In his analysis, Sufism is reduced to individual experience and never opens out onto historical reality, except for the personal “history” of the individual having the experience.
And when it does look beyond that individual, it finds only other individual “experiences.”
Al-Fārābī, the first subject to which Madkūr applies his method, is presented as a Sufi who represents “the earliest form of Sufi ideas among the philosophers of Islam.”
Madkūr divides the influences on al-Fārābī’s Sufism into two kinds: internal and external.
The internal influence is that al-Fārābī “lived a life of asceticism and austerity and preferred solitude and seclusion.”
But what is the source of that?
The first external influence is “the environment in which Abū Naṣr lived.”
At this point, we expect something new. We expect Madkūr to show us the social environment of al-Fārābī’s time and explain how that environment contributed to his Sufism.
But we soon discover that by “environment” he means only the many Sufi ideas circulating in the Islamic world during al-Fārābī’s lifetime.
And the only “historical” explanation he offers for those ideas is that they came from “Indian, Persian, African, or Christian origins.”
The second external influence on al-Fārābī’s Sufism is that he lived at the same time as major Sufis who believed in divine indwelling, such as al-Junayd, al-Shiblī, and al-Ḥallāj.
The third is that al-Fārābī’s theory of happiness was taken from Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics.
The fourth is that he was influenced by Plotinus’s theory of “ecstasy.”
After listing these “external” influences, Madkūr reaches the following conclusion:

“We can therefore see that al-Fārābī’s theory of happiness arose from several factors and different circumstances. It owes as much to al-Fārābī’s own inclinations and dispositions as it does to his environment and to the Muslim thinkers around him.”

This conclusion, together with everything that comes before it, shows us what Madkūr really means by “environment,” “social conditions,” and “surroundings” when he uses these terms in the main outline of his “historical” method.
In the end, the method we were told was historical turns out not to be historical at all.

We have spent this much time on Madkūr’s “historical” method because it represents a trend in contemporary studies of the heritage that has emerged more recently, after the traditionalist method came under growing pressure to change its old ways.
New approaches began to appear that borrowed the forms and language of scientific method, which in our own time has been gaining ground across many areas of research and thought.
But the older traditionalist method still has a powerful influence, even in its older forms.
Let us therefore look at some other examples of approaches that continue to appear in new books and in widely read Arab journals.
In one modern traditionalist work, we find a discussion of the relationship between Arab-Islamic culture and the other cultures it came into contact with and absorbed.
The relationship is described in the following way:

● During the time of ʿUmar, the Arabs conquered a number of different kingdoms and came into contact with very different cultures: Egypt, with the remains of Alexandria, then a center of learning; Persia and Iraq, both rich in different religious and philosophical movements such as Nestorianism, Mazdakism, and Manichaeism; and Syria, where the Sabians and other followers of ancient religions lived...
